title: The chariot leaves Ayodhya
hookLine: a king runs after a chariot, and his son keeps going: why Hindus call Rama maryada purushottama

cards: Look back, and you can't leave. Don't look back, and it feels cruel. That's the trouble with driving away from someone standing in a doorway, and it's Rama's trouble now.
The charioteer Sumantra has the horses ready. Rama, Sita and Lakshmana climb in, with their weapons, a spade, a basket, and Sita's clothes for fourteen years.
As the chariot starts to roll, the whole city starts to run after it.

teach.h: THE CITY RUNS BESIDE THE WHEELS.
teach.b: Valmiki fills the streets with noise. People run beside the wheels, calling to Sumantra to slow down so they can see Rama's face a little longer.
From the palace comes the old king himself, on foot, with Kausalya, crying: wait, Sumantra, wait. Rama hears his father. He can't bear it, and he can't stop.
Go on, he tells the driver quietly.

If the king asks later, say you didn't hear. Being told to stop and told to go is pain either way; better to make it short. The chariot pulls away, and Dasharatha watches until even the dust from the wheels is gone.

But the people keep following, all the way to the Tamasa river, and the whole crowd sleeps on the bank around them. Rama lies awake. These people will follow us into the forest, he thinks, and lose their homes.
So before dawn he and Sumantra harness the horses quietly, cross the river, and turn the chariot back and forth so the tracks can't be followed. Here's why Hindus treasure this scene.
Rama's father is begging him to stop, and he doesn't, because stopping would break the word his father gave. Hindus call Rama maryada purushottama, the best of men, who keeps the bounds.
Maryada is the line dharma draws, and Rama keeps it even when love is pulling the other way. But look how he keeps it: a goodbye made short, and a whole city spared.

In the Ramayana, dharma is firm and kind at once. It's why Hindu families still hold Rama up as the one who keeps his word: hold the line you've promised, and spare the people you love what pain you can.

how: In the text, the departure from Ayodhya moves slowly, and its lasting image is the old king watching the road until even the dust of the wheels is gone.

games.q: the road out — tap the pairs.
p: the river where the crowd sleeps
watches until the dust is gone

s: Rama stops the chariot when his father calls
he tells Sumantra to go on, and to say he didn't hear.
the people of Ayodhya follow Rama to the Tamasa river
and the crowd sleeps on the bank around him.
Rama keeps going because he doesn't care about his father
he keeps the word his father gave. that's maryada: dharma's line, kept even through tears.

games.q: you're Rama. your father, in tears, calls stop. but stopping would break the word he gave. by maryada, what do you do?
o: stop; your father's tears come first.
go on, and keep the goodbye short.
turn back and argue for the throne.
games.why: he goes on, because the given word is dharma's line, and he keeps it kindly: a short goodbye, then a whole crowd spared before dawn.

practice: Many Hindus say Rama's name when the road is hard: just Ram, softly. If you pray, let it ride your out-breath for a few minutes, Ram, and rest in the in-breath between.
If you don't pray, think of a goodbye you had to make; breathe in the pull to look back, breathe out the line you kept.

wordCard.voice: The departure, part three: the road. Rama keeps his father's word while his father weeps, then slips away before dawn to spare the people. That's maryada.

orig.note: Sanskrit tamasā: the river where Rama spends his first night of exile, and where the crowd that followed him sleeps.

carryVoice: Your line: maryada: keep dharma's line, gently. Firm on the word, kind to the people. See you tomorrow.
